Sequential optimization is difficult in this setting because it can distort both individual class representatives and their relative geometry, especially when vibration patterns also vary with operating conditions. We introduce graph continual prototype learning (GCPL), which represents each observed class by a prototype and connects related prototypes through a sparse feature-space graph. New-class samples initialize new nodes and local edges, whereas node- and edge-stability terms constrain changes to the previously learned class structure. The graph is learned from embeddings rather than predefined fault taxonomies, and its retained state scales with the number of classes instead of the number of vibration windows. A leakage-resistant evaluation protocol is specified for four public bearing datasets and jointly measures cumulative-class accuracy, old-class forgetting, new-class learning, and robustness to operating-condition shifts. This formulation provides a compact pattern-recognition framework for studying relational structure in replay-free incremental categories that appear after deployment, while retaining historical vibration records may be restricted by storage, privacy, or maintenance constraints. This paper addresses the resulting replay-free class-incremental vibration fault diagnosis problem. We propose graph continual prototype learning (GCPL), a compact AI-based diagnostic framework that stores class prototypes, diagonal dispersion estimates, and a sparse relation graph instead of previous signal windows. New classes are inserted locally, while prototype anchoring, old-edge consistency, neighborhood-rank preservation, reliability weighting, and a topology-aware boundary margin constrain destabilization of the retained class structure. Record- or bearing-level splits are applied before windowing on CWRU, Paderborn, XJTU-SY, and JNU to avoid overlapping-window leakage. Across four datasets and five matched seeds, GCPL attains AIA values of 95.1%, 91.2%, 89.5%, and 92.4%, improving on the strongest replay-free baseline by 2.1\u20132.6 points and reducing final-session forgetting by 1.8\u20132.3 points. Additional tests cover relation drift, operating-condition shift, additive noise, low-shot and long-tail increments, class order, calibration, and retained-state efficiency. The results indicate that preserving inter-class topology is an effective compact memory mechanism for adaptive vibration monitoring.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.7315097","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Relation-preserving graph continual prototype learning for replay-free class-incremental vibration fault diagnosis"],"author":[{"given":"qinao","family":"hu","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.7315097"},{"abstract":"Replay-based Federated Class-Incremental Learning (FCIL) faces two critical limitations: Each client's replay buffer stores its own historical samples, preventing crucial knowledge from being transferred across clients. Privacy information can be uncovered by millions or billions of parameters, and the upload of parameter updates to server is extremely high-exhausting. To overcome these challenges, we propose \\textbf{FedCACH}: a novel method that \\textbf{Fed}eratively \\textbf{CACH}es regularized pseudo-word embeddings uploaded to the server to facilitate cross-client knowledge transfer with manageable communication and computation\u00a0 costs. Specifically, FedCACH leverages diffusion models for bidirectional text-image conversion. Clients perform regularized image-to-text prompt learning to generate regularized pseudo-word embeddings. They represent client knowledge with respect to client privacy. The server aggregates and caches these regularized pseudo-word embeddings into a buffer, using them as knowledgeable guidance cues for text-to-image synthesis. The resulting synthetic images, embodying aggregated cross-client knowledge, are used to replay in server-side incremental tasks. The replayed global model is then redistributed to clients for personalized finetuning. Experiments demonstrate the feasibility and privacy of client-side prompt learning under moderate computation budgets. We substantiate FedCACH's superiority over existing FCIL methods in mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enhancing incremental learning performance.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.7493948","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Replay on Server: Text-Image Bidirectional Conversion for Federated Class-Incremental imbalance pose major challenges in continual learning for critical care. Predictive models must safely adapt to incoming patient data. In this paper, we introduce Balanced-Reservoir Replay (BRR), a simple modification to reservoir sampling that preserves minority-class examples when the buffer is full. We evaluated BRR on the eICU-CRD dataset (2,520 patients, 8.37% mortality) using only age and gender, in a task-incremental setup with eight tasks and buffer sizes ranging from 0 to 1000 samples.Using a 1000-sample buffer (~\u200940% of past data), BRR outperformed standard sequential training, achieving an average AUC of 0.628\u2009\u00b1\u20090.019 compared to 0.610\u2009\u00b1\u20090.016 (p\u2009<\u20090.01). It also reduced forgetting by 16% (0.106\u2009\u00b1\u20090.047 vs. 0.126\u2009\u00b1\u20090.066), which narrowed the gap with cumulative training by 39%. A clinical composite score, which penalized forgetting twice as much as accuracy gains (\u03bb\u2009=\u20092.0), indicated that a buffer size of 1000 was optimal. We conducted a sensitivity analysis of eight configurations of training duration (40 vs. 80 epochs per task) and forgetting penalties (\u03bb\u2009=\u20090.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0) supported the validity of this selection.This work questions the idea of minimal memory in continual learning. It indicates that retaining some past data can improve accuracy, enhance stability, and help meet regulatory requirements for slowly changing, low-data clinical tasks. BRR only needs about 50 KB of data, and it\u2019s easy to understand and use in places where resources are limited. While recent advances have improved generation fidelity and robustness, most existing approaches implicitly assume that replay is equally beneficial across samples, classes, or tasks. We revisit generative replay from a utility-guided perspective and ask two questions: which samples should be generated within each class, and how should the replay budget be allocated across past tasks? To this end, we study these questions in a feature-space replay setting and propose two complementary mechanisms. First, an intra-class utility module steers generation toward informative regions of the class distribution by considering uncertainty, representativeness, and diversity. Second, an inter-task allocation module adaptively distributes the replay budget across previously learned tasks based on measurable signals of forgetting and interference. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-100 under different class-incremental protocols show that the proposed method consistently improves incremental accuracy and reduces forgetting.
